blocks.text: The cheap phone charger sold in Computer Village, the LED bulb that replaced the tungsten lamp in a Lagos sitting room, and the inverter that keeps a shop's lights on during a PHCN outage all depend on one idea: a semiconductor diode that lets current through one way and blocks it the other. That is how a.c. from the wall becomes d.c. for electronics.

blocks.markdown:
Solids are classed by how easily electrons can move, which in band theory means the size of the **energy gap** between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band.

- **Conductors** (copper, aluminium): valence and conduction bands overlap, or the valence band is only partly filled. Electrons are free at room temperature. Resistivity is very low.
- **Insulators** (rubber, glass, dry wood): the gap is large (several eV). Almost no electrons reach the conduction band. Resistivity is very high.
- **Semiconductors** (silicon, germanium): the gap is small (about 1 eV for Si). A few electrons are thermally excited across the gap, leaving **holes** behind. Resistivity sits between the other two and **falls** as temperature rises — the opposite of a metal.

blocks.caption: The same silicon crystal can be made far more conducting by doping, which is the next step.

blocks.title: Doping
blocks.text: Doping is the controlled addition of a tiny amount of impurity to an intrinsic (pure) semiconductor to increase its conductivity and to choose the majority carrier.

blocks.markdown:
### n-type and p-type

Silicon and germanium are tetravalent: each atom shares four electrons.

- **n-type**: add a **pentavalent donor** (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony). Four electrons bond; the fifth is loosely bound and becomes a free electron. Majority carriers are **electrons** (negative); minority carriers are holes.
- **p-type**: add a **trivalent acceptor** (boron, aluminium, gallium, indium). The impurity has only three bonding electrons, so a **hole** appears. Majority carriers are **holes** (positive); minority carriers are electrons.

The crystal as a whole stays electrically neutral: n-type is not negatively charged overall, and p-type is not positively charged overall.

blocks.title: Identifying the semiconductor type
blocks.prompt: A pure silicon crystal is doped with a small quantity of phosphorus. State the type of semiconductor produced, name the majority carrier, and explain why conductivity rises.

steps.text: Phosphorus is in group V, so it is pentavalent — a donor impurity.
Four of its five outer electrons form bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms; the fifth is easily freed into the conduction band.
The crystal is therefore n-type, with electrons as majority carriers (and holes as minority carriers).
Extra free electrons mean a much higher charge-carrier density than in intrinsic silicon, so conductivity increases.

blocks.answer: n-type silicon; majority carriers are electrons; conductivity rises because donor atoms add free electrons

blocks.markdown:
### The p–n junction diode and rectification

Join p-type to n-type and electrons diffuse into the p-side, holes into the n-side. They recombine near the join and leave a **depletion layer** stripped of free carriers, with a built-in barrier potential.

- **Forward bias**: p-side to the positive terminal, n-side to the negative. The barrier is reduced, the depletion layer thins, and a large current flows.
- **Reverse bias**: connections swapped. The barrier rises, the depletion layer widens, and only a tiny minority-carrier current flows. The diode is 'off'.

That one-way behaviour is **rectification**: converting a.c. to d.c.

- **Half-wave**: one diode in series with the load. Only alternate half-cycles pass; the other halves are blocked. The output is pulsing d.c. with gaps.
- **Full-wave**: a bridge of four diodes (or a centre-tap transformer with two diodes) uses both half-cycles. The output still pulses, but without the gaps, and is easier to smooth with a capacitor.

An **LED** is a p–n junction made from a compound semiconductor. In forward bias, electrons recombine with holes and emit photons — the light of LED bulbs and phone indicators.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Forward bias: arrow of the diode symbol points with conventional current (p to n). Donor = pentavalent = n-type = electrons; acceptor = trivalent = p-type = holes. Half-wave uses one diode; full-wave bridge uses four. And conductivity of a semiconductor rises with temperature — the metallic-conductor instinct is the usual trap.

points: Conductors have overlapping or partly filled bands; insulators have a large band gap; semiconductors have a small gap and conductivity that rises with temperature.
n-type: pentavalent donor (P, As); majority carriers are electrons. p-type: trivalent acceptor (B, Al); majority carriers are holes.
A p–n junction has a depletion layer. Forward bias conducts; reverse bias blocks.
A diode rectifies a.c.: half-wave (one diode) or full-wave (bridge of four).
An LED is a forward-biased p–n junction that emits light when electrons recombine with holes.
